title: Maximum period for which undertrial prisoner can be detained

content.overview: BNSS s. 479, Maximum period for which undertrial prisoner can be detained, is a procedural provision in the Provisions as to bail and bonds cluster. content.study:
Current-law identity
BNSS s. 479 governs maximum period for which undertrial prisoner can be detained within Chapter XXXV - Provisions as to bail and bonds. The provision must be read with its enacted sub-sections, provisos, explanations, the BNSS First Schedule where classification or trial forum is relevant, and BNSS s. 478, BNSS s. 480. Historical concordance: CrPC s. 436A.

Procedural meaning and legislative purpose
Criminal procedure is a sequence of safeguards, not a collection of isolated powers. This section allocates a procedural step to the police, Magistrate, trial court, Sessions Court or High Court and places conditions around its exercise. The mischief addressed is identified from the statutory text and Chapter setting; the court should not add a condition that the legislature did not enact or remove a safeguard that the text requires.

Mandatory application checklist
1. Identify the proceeding, procedural stage and order sought.
2. Confirm whether the investigation, inquiry, trial, application or appeal was pending immediately before 1 July 2024. If so, begin with BNSS s. 531(2)(a) and test whether the saved CrPC route governs.
3. Quote the exact operative words of s. 479, including every condition, proviso and explanation.
4. Identify the competent criminal court, territorial rule, statutory sanction or classification requirement.
5. Map each material fact to the statutory condition it proves or fails.
6. State the immediate remedy and the standard for interference.

Evidence and constitutional control
The procedural record remains subject to Articles 14, 20, 21 and 22 of the Constitution. The party asserting a factual foundation bears the ordinary burden under BSA s. 104; BSA s. 106 is limited to facts especially within a person's knowledge after the foundation is established. Electronic records must be separately tested under BSA s. 63 for the applicable certificate and production requirements. BSA admissibility does not cure an unlawful arrest, search, remand or other BNSS defect.

Courtroom method
In a written submission, state the current section first, identify the stage and forum, reproduce only the necessary statutory language, address the transition rule, apply each condition to the record, answer the principal objection, and request a precise order. Do not treat a police report as proof of guilt, an arrest as a conviction, a charge as a finding, or a procedural irregularity as automatically destroying the entire prosecution.

sections.body:

Read it with BNSS s. 478, BNSS s. 480. A connected section may define the condition, forum, time limit or remedy without replacing this section.
Use historical concordance only to explain development, never as the current citation.

sections.heading: Mandatory Procedural Ingredients and Stage Test
sections.body:
First ingredient: the proceeding must be at the statutory stage addressed by s. 479.
Second ingredient: the competent officer or court must possess the relevant jurisdiction and power.
Third ingredient: each express condition, notice, reason, time limit, record or hearing requirement must be satisfied.
Fourth ingredient: the requested consequence must follow from the proved procedural breach or compliance; state the exact order sought.

sections.heading: BSA 2023 Burden and Electronic Evidence Checkpoints
sections.body:
BSA s. 104 supplies the ordinary burden framework; do not shift the initial burden merely by invoking s. 106.
BSA s. 106 applies to a fact especially within knowledge only after the party relying on the legal proposition establishes the necessary foundation.
Where electronic material is tendered, separately examine relevance, authenticity, integrity, source and BSA s. 63 certificate requirements.

sections.heading: Procedural Roadmap, Forum, Limitation and Transition
sections.body:
For proceedings under the post-1 July 2024 regime, cite BNSS s. 479 and verify the First Schedule or special statute where applicable.
For a matter pending immediately before commencement, apply BNSS s. 531(2)(a) and identify the saved CrPC procedure before addressing merits.
Check the applicable BNSS or special-statute limitation rule and calculate the remedy period from the actual order or event.

cases.name: Lalita Kumari v. Government of Uttar Pradesh
cases.facts: The petitioner sought registration of information disclosing a cognizable offence.
cases.issue: Whether registration is mandatory when information discloses a cognizable offence.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Registration is mandatory when the information discloses a cognizable offence, subject to the limited preliminary-inquiry framework recognised by the Constitution Bench.
cases.holding: The Court directed compliance with mandatory registration and confined preliminary inquiry to recognised categories.
cases.relevance: Use only where s. 479 concerns information, investigation or a connected pre-cognizance step; do not treat this case as authority for every BNSS provision.

cases.name: Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar
cases.facts: The case concerned arrest and detention for an offence carrying imprisonment up to seven years.
cases.issue: Whether arrest and remand may be authorised mechanically in a lower-punishment case.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Police must satisfy and record the necessity conditions for arrest, and Magistrates must not authorise detention mechanically.
cases.holding: The Court issued safeguards enforcing the discipline now reflected in the BNSS arrest framework.
cases.relevance: Use where s. 479 concerns arrest, custody, remand or liberty; otherwise identify a section-specific authority instead of forcing this case into the argument.

cases.name: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal
cases.facts: The Court addressed custodial violence and the absence of reliable arrest safeguards.
cases.issue: What minimum protections must accompany arrest and detention.
cases.ratioDecidendi: Arrest and custody require transparent documentation, accountability and safeguards protecting Articles 21 and 22.
cases.holding: The Court prescribed arrest and custody safeguards that inform the corresponding BNSS duties.
cases.relevance: Use where s. 479 directly engages arrest, custody, production or custody records; do not cite it as a substitute for the statutory text.

learningObjectives: Master the statutory framework for release of undertrial prisoners who have undergone maximum detention under Section 479 BNSS.
Analyze the groundbreaking reform under the first proviso to Section 479(1): mandatory release on personal bond for first-time offenders who have completed one-third of the maximum imprisonment.
Understand the general rule under Section 479(1): release on bail upon completing one-half of the maximum imprisonment.
Examine the statutory exceptions: non-application to offences carrying death penalty or life imprisonment, or persons facing multiple charges/trials.
Evaluate the statutory duty imposed on the Jail Superintendent under Section 479(3) to make written applications to the court for release.
enhancement.definition: BNSS s. 479 provides statutory relief for undertrial prisoners detained for long periods, replacing Section 436A CrPC. Where an undertrial prisoner has undergone detention for a period extending up to one-half of the maximum period of imprisonment specified for that offence, he shall be released by the Court on bail. Under the first proviso, where such person is a first-time offender (who has never been convicted of any offence in the past), he shall be released on bond by the Court if he has undergone detention for the period extending up to one-third of the maximum period of imprisonment. Under sub-section (3), the Superintendent of the jail where the person is detained is statutorily mandated to submit an application to the Court for release upon completion of the requisite period.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Right to speedy trial, prevention of punitive pre-trial incarceration, and decongestion of prisons under Article 21. Pre-trial detention must not be allowed to become a punishment in itself, and first-time offenders are entitled to expedited release on personal bond.
statutoryFramework: Chapter XXXV — Provisions as to Bail and Bonds, BNSS s. 479.
Sub-section (1) General Rule: Release on bail upon undergoing detention extending to one-half of the maximum sentence.
Proviso 1 to Sub-section (1): First-Time Offender Relief — mandatory release on bond upon undergoing one-third of the maximum sentence.
Proviso 2 to Sub-section (1): Judicial discretion to order continued detention beyond one-half/one-third after hearing the Public Prosecutor, with recorded reasons.
Proviso 3 to Sub-section (1): Absolute Bar — in no case shall a person be detained beyond the maximum period of imprisonment provided for the offence.
Sub-section (2): Non-application to offences carrying death or life imprisonment, or where an investigation/trial is pending against the person in multiple cases.
Sub-section (3): Institutional Duty on Jail Superintendent to apply to the Court for release of eligible undertrials.
essentialIngredients: The person is an undertrial prisoner detained in custody during an investigation, inquiry, or trial.
The offence charged does not carry the punishment of death or life imprisonment as specified under sub-section (2).
The person is not undergoing investigation, inquiry, or trial in more than one offence or in multiple cases.
(a) First-time offender: has undergone one-third of the maximum imprisonment prescribed by law; or
(b) Other undertrials: has undergone one-half of the maximum imprisonment prescribed by law.
Statutory release on bail or personal bond, which can only be denied by a reasoned written order after hearing the Public Prosecutor.
enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Section 479 BNSS is one of the most humanitarian provisions in India’s criminal procedural reforms, addressing the chronic crisis of undertrial incarceration where over 70% of prison inmates are awaiting trial.

Replacing Section 436A of the 1973 Code, Section 479 introduces a revolutionary benefit for **first-time offenders**. Under the old law, every undertrial had to serve at least half (50%) of the maximum sentence before becoming eligible for statutory release. Section 479(1) first proviso recognizes that first-time offenders (persons with no prior criminal convictions) are particularly vulnerable to prison contamination. It mandates that a first-time offender **shall be released on bond if he has undergone one-third (33.3%) of the maximum sentence**.

For instance, if an accused with no prior convictions is charged with cheating under Section 318(4) BNS (carrying a maximum of 7 years imprisonment), the accused is entitled to mandatory release after undergoing 2 years and 4 months (one-third) of detention, rather than waiting for 3.5 years.

For undertrials who have prior convictions, the standard half-sentence (50%) rule applies.

Crucially, Section 479(3) addresses the structural failure of the past where indigent prisoners languished unaware of their rights. It places an **affirmative statutory duty on the Superintendent of the jail** to calculate detention periods and immediately submit a written application to the court for the release of eligible prisoners.
examples: Teaching illustration (First-Time Offender 1/3rd Rule): A college student with no criminal record is arrested for an offence punishable with three years imprisonment. Due to judicial backlog, the trial drags on. After the student spends exactly 12 months (one year = 1/3rd of 3 years) in jail, the Jail Superintendent files an application under Section 479(3). Under the first proviso to Section 479(1), the Magistrate is statutorily mandated to release the student on a personal bond.

Teaching illustration (Disqualification Due to Multiple Cases): An undertrial has spent 2.5 years in jail for an offence punishable with 5 years (one-half). He applies for release under Section 479. The prosecution demonstrates that the accused is concurrently facing trial in three separate murder and robbery cases across two other districts. Under Section 479(2), because the person is facing trial in more than one offence and multiple cases, the statutory benefit of Section 479 does not apply.
distinctions: BNSS s. 479 vs CrPC 1973 s. 436A: CrPC s. 436A only recognized the 1/2 detention rule for all prisoners; BNSS s. 479 creates a special 1/3rd detention threshold for first-time offenders and imposes an affirmative duty on the Jail Superintendent to initiate the application.

Section 479 Release vs Default Bail (s. 187): Default bail under Section 187 applies when the police fail to file a chargesheet within 60/90 days during investigation; Section 479 applies during the ongoing trial when total incarceration exceeds 1/3rd or 1/2 of the statutory sentence.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether a first-time offender facing trial for an offence punishable with six years imprisonment, who has been in custody for two years and two months, is entitled to immediate release under Section 479 BNSS.

Rule: Under the first proviso to Section 479(1) BNSS, a first-time offender who has never been convicted in the past is entitled to release on personal bond upon undergoing one-third of the maximum sentence (which is 2 years for a 6-year offence).
Application: The accused is a first-time offender, has no other pending cases, and has served 2 years and 2 months (exceeding the one-third threshold of 2 years).
Conclusion: The accused has an enforceable statutory right to release on personal bond under Section 479(1) proviso; the court must direct release.

keyTakeaways: Section 479 BNSS mandates release of undertrial prisoners who have served half of the maximum imprisonment.
First-time offenders are entitled to mandatory release on personal bond after serving one-third of the maximum sentence.
Does not apply to offences carrying death or life imprisonment, or persons facing trial in multiple cases.
Jail Superintendents are statutorily required to identify eligible prisoners and apply for their release.
